name: Amethyst
description: Look at this pretty stone! It is likely amethyst, a very popular purple type of quartz. Do you see the white stripes cutting through the purple parts? This creates a beautiful chevron pattern. Amethyst gets its lovely purple color from tiny bits of iron trapped inside the crystal while it was growing deep underground millions of years ago.
alt_text: A polished, rounded purple and white stone with V-shaped chevron patterns resting on a dark, wood-textured surface.
uncertainty_note: Without a hardness test, it is difficult to distinguish polished amethyst quartz from fluorite, though the chevron pattern strongly suggests amethyst.

name: Fluorite
description: Look closely at this pretty, mint-green stone! This is likely fluorite, a very special mineral. Did you know that some fluorite specimens can actually glow under a blacklight? This cool trick is called fluorescence, and scientists named the glow after this exact mineral! Its smooth, angled surfaces show how it breaks along neat, straight lines.
alt_text: A small, rough chunk of translucent, light green mineral with fractured, glassy surfaces, resting on a dark, textured wood-like background.
uncertainty_note: Many translucent green minerals, like fluorite, calcite, or aventurine, can look very similar without chemical or physical hardness testing.
privacy_note: No privacy risks are visible in this photograph of a mineral specimen on a table.

name: Sodalite
description: Look at this beautiful blue specimen! It looks a lot like a mineral called sodalite, which is famous for its rich royal blue color mixed with white streaks. Sodalite gets its name because it contains a lot of sodium inside it. Artists sometimes carve this tough, colorful stone into pretty beads, jewelry, and small statues.
alt_text: A small, rough, triangular piece of blue mineral with white streaks and a crystalline texture, resting on a dark wooden surface.
uncertainty_note: Visually, this specimen closely resembles sodalite or lapis lazuli, but definitive identification requires mineralogical testing.
